sections.description: Matthew frames the core dilemma: finish a first indie game and make a business out of it within about a year, or risk losing momentum. He introduces 1849 as the launch example and outlines the shift from multiple concepts to a single-year plan.
sections.title: Introduction, stakes, and year-long planning

sections.description: The team adopts swag scheduling (stupid, wild-ass guests), breaks work into chunks, and estimates duration and cost. They perform a meta calculation that yields roughly 16 months of work, then apply butchery to cut the most time-consuming parts (notably, a multiplayer system).
sections.title: Swag scheduling and initial project breakdown

sections.description: Butchered scope reveals a 4-month multiplayer effort; they cut to sole focus on single-player. They opt for familiar Flash tooling over Unity to minimize risk, and emphasize careful contractor onboarding, documentation, and corporate formation.
sections.title: Risk reduction, tech choices, and contractor management

sections.description: Nine months in, they begin self-marketing, frame publicity as strategic (not magic), and build a community via devlogs, social media, and targeted outreach. They discuss the roles of journalists and platforms like Rock, Paper, Shotgun (RP$), YouTubers, and non-game media.
sections.title: Marketing groundwork, community building, and journalist outreach

sections.description: The team leverages devlogs and cross-posts, uses Indie Game Stand for early access, and highlights the value of testing with a smaller community before a broad Steam release.
sections.title: Audience engagement channels and early access strategy

sections.description: They plan a simultaneous multi-platform launch, discuss distinct game stories for PC and mobile, weigh pricing tensions, and introduce a cross-platform pricing dilemma, emphasizing justification of PC pricing and content differentiation.
sections.title: Cross-platform release planning and pricing tensions

sections.description: The talk reviews revenue sources (roughly 60% PC, 40% mobile), the impact of German and French localizations, and the importance of appearing on multiple stores. They note localization shifts (German becoming a top market after translation).
sections.title: Localization, platform stores, and revenue mix

sections.description: Marketing continues after launch: DLC bumps sales, ads are used with urgency and consistent voice, and ‘the tail’ is actively flogged through promotions and ongoing content.
sections.title: Post-release marketing, DLC, and ad strategy

sections.description: They outline bootstrapping, the plan for a second game (two-year horizon), and how urgency persists. Q&A touches on investor avoidance, early tester networks, and contracting via personal networks.
sections.title: Second game and takeaways, Q&A highlights

summary: In this GDC Festival of Gaming presentation, SomaSim cofounder Matthew Vione recounts how his studio planned, produced, marketed, and self-published their first indie simulation game, 1849, within a year (ultimately ~14 months). The talk emphasizes pragmatic project scoping (swag scheduling and the “butchery” cut of features), risk management (sticking to familiar tech), contract and corporate basics, and a multi-faceted self-marketing plan that includes devlogs, social-media outreach, press relations, influencer engagement, and non-game media hooks. The team pursued a cross-platform release (PC and mobile) with careful pricing decisions and localization to boost long-tail sales, while also leveraging early access, DLC, and periodic ads to sustain revenue after launch. The talk culminates with lessons on how to sustain a new studio’s momentum after their first release, and how the second project is structured to avoid over-reliance on the first success.
title: One-Year Indie Game Launch: Planning, Production, and Self-Publishing (SomaSim's 1849 Case Study)
